On the deck, Vladimir Mayakovsky in his signature yellow jacket and wide tie, gesturing dramatically with one hand raised, face full of revolutionary fervor. Around him, oversized books with the names Pushkin and Tolstoy on their spines are being tipped over the railing. One book (Pushkin) is mid‑fall, another (Tolstoy) tilting dangerously. In the water below, the books create exaggerated cartoonish splashes. Background: industrial early‑Soviet cityscape with smokestacks and angular buildings, muted earthy tones with pops of red. Subtle humor in the exaggerated expressions and motion lines. High detail in textures: paper grain of the books, fabric folds of Mayakovsky’s jacket, chalky strokes. No text or readable letters.

16:9 image. Medium: colored pencils and chalk. Style: narrative illustration with a touch of gentle satire. In the foreground, Mayakovsky (easily recognizable by his height, yellow attire, and intense expression) stands next to a giant lever labeled (visually, not with text) as “modernity”. He’s pulling it with great effort. As the lever moves, a large bookshelf on the other side tilts, and books by Pushkin and Tolstoy slide off dramatically. The books are oversized compared to Mayakovsky to emphasize the weight of tradition. Pushkin’s book has a tiny crown icon embossed on the cover; Tolstoy’s book features a subtle silhouette of a horse and carriage. Background: a modest literary salon turned into a workshop of revolution—bookshelves, old lamps, typewriter, all slightly askew. Warm, vintage palette with chalky highlights and pencil outlines. Emotion: Mayakovsky looks determined but also slightly absurd in his effort. No legible text or letters.

16:9 image. Medium: colored pencils and chalk, hand‑drawn look with deliberate imperfections and visible outlines. In the center, Mayakovsky is straining to push a monument of Pushkin off its pedestal; his face is full of revolutionary zeal, but his posture is awkward, as if the monument is heavier than expected. The statue of Pushkin is tilted, and its face looks mildly offended yet dignified. A second monument of Tolstoy lies on the ground nearby, slightly tilted, with a tiny open book and a pair of reading glasses resting beside it, as if Tolstoy just stepped away for a moment. Background: a simplified city square with a few trees and lampposts, rendered with loose sketchy lines. The humor comes from the contrast between Mayakovsky’s intensity and the calm, almost indifferent demeanor of the monuments. Warm browns, greys, and ochre with red highlights. No text.

The palette is limited: dark grey for monuments, bright ochre for Mayakovsky’s jacket, and deep red for key accents.
